# Assembling the Compendium {#sec-zzcollab}

A collaborator clones your compendium, restores the lockfile,
renders the paper, and gets a p-value of 0.06 where the manuscript
reports 0.04. Every package version matches yours. The difference
is in the data: the repository could not hold the outcomes file,
the README said to copy it from the shared drive, and the shared
drive now holds a later extract with corrections. Nothing failed,
and nothing in the repository could tell either of you that the
inputs differed. A compendium reproduces an answer only when every
layer the answer depends on is pinned, and this chapter is the
checklist for those layers, the Five Pillars, with the ways to
assemble and audit them.


operations which we can perform without thinking about them.*

## The Five Pillars {#sec-zzcollab-pillars}

The preceding chapters each solved one layer of the
reproducibility problem and each left the wiring to you. A
compendium (@sec-rrtools) does not come with a lockfile; a
lockfile (@sec-renv) does not come with a container; a container
(@sec-docker) does not know where your data came from. The Five
Pillars are the checklist that says when the wiring is complete.
They are tool-neutral: the same five hold whether you assemble
them by hand or let a framework do it, and @tbl-five-pillars
states what each pins and what goes wrong without it.

| Pillar | Pins | Without it | Check |
|---|---|---|---|
| Dockerfile | Operating system, system libraries, the R build | Packages restore onto a different R or BLAS (Basic Linear Algebra Subprograms), and the last digits of an estimate move | The base image's R version equals the lockfile's |
| `renv.lock` | The exact version and source of every R package | A changed default in an upgraded package changes a number without an error | `renv::status()` reports no issues |
| `.Rprofile` | Activation of the project library at startup | R loads your global library instead, and the lockfile is silently bypassed | `.libPaths()[1]` is inside `renv/library` where you render |
| Source code | The analysis itself, in `R/` and `analysis/` | Nothing to rerun, or a version nobody can identify | Committed to Git, and the submitted version tagged |
| Data | The inputs: raw files, or a documented path to them | A later extract gives a different answer from the same code | A committed checksum manifest verifies |

: The Five Pillars as a tool-neutral checklist. A compendium
missing any one is incomplete. {#tbl-five-pillars}

The pillars are easier to remember as a stack than as a list,
because each one captures a layer the one above it takes for
granted. @fig-five-pillars is that stack.

```{mermaid}
%%| echo: false
%%| label: fig-five-pillars
%%| fig-alt: "Five layers stacked bottom to top, each depending on
%%|   the one below. From the bottom: the Dockerfile supplying
%%|   operating system, system libraries and the R build; renv.lock
%%|   pinning every R package version; .Rprofile activating the
%%|   project library; the source code in R/ and analysis/; and at
%%|   the top the data, raw and derived or a documented path to
%%|   it."
%%| fig-cap: "The Five Pillars as a layered stack. Each layer
%%|   assumes the one beneath it. Remove the Dockerfile and the R
%%|   packages have no operating system to install onto; remove the
%%|   lockfile and the source code has no packages; remove the data
%%|   and there is nothing to analyze."
flowchart TD
  D["<b>5. Data</b><br/><i>raw and derived, or a documented path to them</i>"]
  S["<b>4. Source code</b><br/><i>the analysis, in R/ and analysis/</i>"]
  P["<b>3. .Rprofile</b><br/><i>activates the project library</i>"]
  L["<b>2. renv.lock</b><br/><i>every R package version</i>"]
  F["<b>1. Dockerfile</b><br/><i>operating system, system libraries, R build</i>"]
  F --> L --> P --> S --> D
```

Two of the pillars need a word more than the table gives them.
The `renv.lock` records the R version as well as every package,
but it does not install R; the R installation comes from the
Dockerfile, which is why the two must agree. And the data pillar
does not require the data to be in the repository. Sensitive data
often cannot live in the compendium; then the compendium holds a
README documenting the access path, in the form @sec-federal sets
out, and a manifest of checksums that lets anyone confirm they
obtained the same files. The opening's failure was a data pillar
with the README and without the manifest.

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'}
**Question.** A project has a Dockerfile and a committed
`renv.lock`, and its `.Rprofile` activates `renv`. Which pillars
does a collaborator still have to take on trust?

**Answer.** Two. The source code is pinned only if it is
committed and the version you reported is tagged; otherwise the
collaborator cannot know which commit produced the paper. And the
data are pinned only if they are in the repository or a manifest
records their checksums; otherwise a later extract produces a
different answer from the same code, with nothing to say so. The
environment pillars cannot detect either problem.
:::

## Assembling the compendium by hand {#sec-zzcollab-assemble}

Assembling the pillars by hand takes about half an hour per
project, and doing it once is the best way to understand what any
framework that automates it is doing for you. Each step uses a
tool from an earlier chapter; the commands below are
display-only, because they create a project on your machine.

1. **Layout and source code.** Scaffold the compendium with
   `rrtools` and put it under Git (@sec-rrtools, @sec-git-solo):

   ```r
   rrtools::use_compendium("~/research/hfhome")
   rrtools::use_analysis()
   ```

   ```bash
   git init
   ```

2. **Lockfile and `.Rprofile`.** Initialize `renv`, which writes
   both, install what the analysis uses, and snapshot
   (@sec-renv):

   ```r
   renv::init()
   renv::snapshot()
   ```

3. **Dockerfile.** Copy the canonical Dockerfile from
   @sec-docker-canonical to the project root, with its
   `.dockerignore`, and set the base image's tag to the R version
   in `renv.lock`. `rrtools::use_dockerfile()` writes a different
   Dockerfile; this book uses the canonical one, so that one file
   is described everywhere.

4. **Data.** Put the raw files in `analysis/data/raw_data/`, or a
   README there that says how to obtain them, and commit a
   checksum manifest of the files (below).

5. **Tag.** Commit, and tag the commit you submit:

   ```bash
   git tag -a v1.0-submission -m "Submitted to journal"
   ```

The manifest is the step most projects skip. It is one line per
file, the file's SHA-256 checksum (a 64-character fingerprint of
its contents) and its path, in the format the `shasum` command
reads and writes, so that you can create it in R and anyone can
check it from a shell. The chunk below assembles a small HF-HOME
compendium in a temporary directory, with the manifest step
deliberately left out and a Dockerfile copied from an older
project, so that the audit in the next section has something to
find.

```{r}
#| label: zzcollab-toy-compendium
hf_dir <- file.path("..", "data", "raw_data", "hfhome")
comp <- file.path(tempdir(), "hfhome-compendium")
unlink(comp, recursive = TRUE)
raw <- file.path(comp, "analysis", "data", "raw_data")
dir.create(raw, recursive = TRUE)
dir.create(file.path(comp, "R"))
invisible(file.copy(
  file.path(hf_dir, c("randomization.csv", "outcomes.csv")), raw
))
writeLines(
  "derive_analysis_set <- function(rand, outc) merge(rand, outc)",
  file.path(comp, "R", "derive.R")
)
writeLines('source("renv/activate.R")', file.path(comp, ".Rprofile"))
writeLines(
  '{"R": {"Version": "4.4.0", "Repositories": []}, "Packages": {}}',
  file.path(comp, "renv.lock")
)
writeLines(c("FROM rocker/r-ver:4.3.1", "WORKDIR /work"),
           file.path(comp, "Dockerfile"))
invisible(system2("git", c("init", "-q", comp)))
list.files(comp, recursive = TRUE, all.files = TRUE,
           include.dirs = FALSE) |>
  grep(pattern = "^[.]git/", invert = TRUE, value = TRUE)
```

Every pillar has a file. Whether every pillar is *pinned* is a
different question, and the listing cannot answer it.

::: {.callout-warning title='Pitfall'}
**An `.Rprofile` that never runs.** R reads `.Rprofile` from the
directory it starts in, then from your home directory. Render from
a subdirectory (`cd analysis/paper`, or an RStudio project rooted
there) and the project's `.Rprofile` at the root never runs: no
error, no message, and the analysis uses your global library while
the lockfile says otherwise. This book hit exactly this, because
Quarto starts R in the directory being rendered; its fix is a
second `.Rprofile` in `analysis/report/` that points `renv` at the
project root. The check in @tbl-five-pillars catches it: run
`.libPaths()[1]` from the directory where you render.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'}
**Question.** Step 3 sets the Dockerfile's base tag to the R
version in `renv.lock`. What happens if the two disagree, and why
is nothing likely to report it?

**Answer.** `renv` restores the recorded package versions onto
whatever R the image supplies. The build usually succeeds, because
most package versions install on a neighboring R, and the analysis
runs. What changes is the layer beneath the packages (R itself,
and the numerical libraries it links), so results can differ in
their last digits from the ones you reported, with no error
anywhere.
:::

## Auditing the pillars {#sec-zzcollab-audit}

A checklist you run by eye drifts; a checklist you run as code
does not. The function below turns @tbl-five-pillars into five
assertions about a project directory. It uses only `renv`, `cli`,
and base R, so it audits a compendium however it was assembled.

```{r}
#| label: zzcollab-audit-fn
audit_pillars <- function(root) {
  path <- function(...) file.path(root, ...)
  lock_r <- if (file.exists(path("renv.lock"))) {
    renv::lockfile_read(path("renv.lock"))$R$Version
  } else {
    NA_character_
  }
  from <- if (file.exists(path("Dockerfile"))) {
    grep("^FROM ", readLines(path("Dockerfile")), value = TRUE)[1]
  } else {
    NA_character_
  }
  rprofile <- if (file.exists(path(".Rprofile"))) {
    readLines(path(".Rprofile"))
  } else {
    character(0)
  }
  code <- list.files(root, pattern = "[.](R|qmd|Rmd)$",
                     recursive = TRUE)
  manifest <- path("data-manifest.sha256")
  data_ok <- file.exists(manifest) && {
    m <- read.table(manifest, col.names = c("sha256", "file"))
    all(vapply(path(m$file), cli::hash_file_sha256, character(1)) ==
          m$sha256)
  }
  data.frame(
    pillar = c("Dockerfile", "renv.lock", ".Rprofile",
               "Source code", "Data"),
    check = c("base image tag equals the lockfile's R version",
              "lockfile present and readable",
              "activates renv",
              "analysis code present, under Git",
              "raw files match the checksum manifest"),
    ok = c(
      !is.na(from) && !is.na(lock_r) &&
        grepl(paste0(":", lock_r, "($|@)"), from),
      !is.na(lock_r),
      any(grepl("renv/activate.R", rprofile, fixed = TRUE)),
      length(code) > 0 && file.exists(path(".git")),
      data_ok
    )
  )
}

audit_pillars(comp)
```

Two pillars fail. The Dockerfile names R 4.3.1 while the lockfile
records 4.4.0, and there is no manifest for the data. Fix both:
set the base tag to the lockfile's version, and write the
manifest.

```{r}
#| label: zzcollab-audit-fix
lock_r <- renv::lockfile_read(file.path(comp, "renv.lock"))$R$Version
writeLines(c(paste0("FROM rocker/r-ver:", lock_r), "WORKDIR /work"),
           file.path(comp, "Dockerfile"))

data_files <- list.files(raw, full.names = TRUE)
writeLines(
  paste0(vapply(data_files, cli::hash_file_sha256, character(1)),
         "  ", file.path("analysis", "data", "raw_data",
                         basename(data_files))),
  file.path(comp, "data-manifest.sha256")
)

audit <- audit_pillars(comp)
audit
```

::: {.callout-tip title='Verification'}
Assert the audit rather than reading it, and confirm from a shell
that the manifest is in the standard format (display-only; run it
in the compendium's root):

```{r}
#| label: zzcollab-audit-verify
stopifnot(all(audit$ok))
```

```bash
shasum -a 256 --check data-manifest.sha256
```

The shell check prints `OK` beside each file. In your own project,
run `audit_pillars(".")` from the root before every tag, and
regenerate the manifest only when you deliberately receive new
data, committing it with the data change.
:::

The audit is a structural check. It confirms that each pillar is
present and consistent; it cannot confirm that the analysis
reproduces. That test is the one in @sec-renv and @sec-docker:
build the image, restore the lockfile, run the analysis from a
fresh clone, and compare the results with the ones you reported.

::: {.callout-important title='LLM prompt'}
A model can map an unfamiliar project onto the pillars quickly.
Give it the files that decide each pillar, not a description.

> **Context.** Below are the output of
> `git ls-files` for an R analysis project, the `FROM` line of its
> Dockerfile, the `R$Version` from its `renv.lock`, and the full
> text of its `.Rprofile`.
>
> **Constraints.** Assess the Five Pillars (Dockerfile,
> `renv.lock`, `.Rprofile`, source code, data) using only these
> inputs. Do not recommend a framework or a template. Do not
> propose moving or editing anything in the raw-data directory.
>
> **Criteria.** For each pillar: present, absent, or present but
> inert, with the line of input that shows it. For each gap, the
> smallest addition that closes it.

*Failure mode.* Models report a pillar as present because a file
with the right name exists: an `.Rprofile` that never activates
`renv`, a Dockerfile whose tag disagrees with the lockfile, a data
README with no checksums. Or they recommend adopting a framework,
which answers a different question. *Check.* Run `audit_pillars()`
on the project and compare its `ok` column with the model's
verdicts. File names and configuration are structure; send no
data files (@sec-ai-governance).
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'}
**Question.** The audit passes on your compendium. A month later a
colleague edits one value in `outcomes.csv` to correct a data
entry error and reruns the analysis. What does the audit report,
and what should happen next?

**Answer.** The data pillar fails, because the file's checksum no
longer matches the manifest. That is the audit doing its job: the
inputs changed, and now someone knows. Raw data are evidence, so
the correction should arrive as a new extract with its provenance
recorded, the manifest regenerated and committed with it, and the
changed result explained, not as a hand edit to the file.
:::

### Exercises

1. In the toy compendium, change one outcome in
   `analysis/data/raw_data/outcomes.csv` and rerun the audit.
   Which pillar fails?

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'}
```{r}
#| label: soln-10-1
outcomes_path <- file.path(raw, "outcomes.csv")
lines <- readLines(outcomes_path)
lines[2] <- sub(",0,", ",1,", lines[2], fixed = TRUE)
writeLines(lines, outcomes_path)
audit_pillars(comp)[c("pillar", "ok")]
```

Only the data pillar fails. A one-character change to one patient
is invisible to every other check, and to anyone reading the
results; the manifest is what makes it loud.
:::

2. Audit this book's own repository with
   `audit_pillars(file.path("..", ".."))` and explain each failure.

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'}
```{r}
#| label: soln-10-2
audit_pillars(file.path("..", ".."))[c("pillar", "ok")]
```

Each `FALSE` is a pillar the book's repository does not supply in
the form the audit checks. A missing Dockerfile means the R
version and system libraries are whatever the reader's machine
has; a missing data manifest means the reader cannot confirm the
files match the ones the book was built from, though here the
HF-HOME files can be regenerated from their seeded script. A book
that teaches the pillars is held to them too.
:::

## Choosing how much to automate {#sec-zzcollab-choosing}

Assembling by hand gives you full control and costs half an hour
per project. It is also exactly the kind of work that gets done
slightly differently every time, which defeats the consistency it
was supposed to produce. Several tools automate parts of it; they
differ in which pillars they supply and in how much of the layout
they decide for you.

| Approach | Supplies | Leaves to you | Suits |
|---|---|---|---|
| By hand | Whatever you choose, as above | Every step, and its consistency across projects | Learning the pillars; a single paper |
| `rrtools` [@marwick2018packaging] | Package-style layout, a Dockerfile, a README | The lockfile, matching the Dockerfile to it, the data manifest | A paper with code, in the community-standard layout |
| `workflowr` [@blischak2019workflowr] | A project website in which each results page records its Git commit and R session information | The lockfile, the container, the data manifest | An analysis that is shared as it develops, as a website |
| `zzcollab` (@sec-zzcollab-optional) | Layout, `renv.lock`, `.Rprofile`, Dockerfile, a `Makefile`, dependency checks | The data manifest's upkeep, and the choice of profile | A group producing many projects that should look alike |

: Ways to assemble a compendium. None removes the audit.
{#tbl-zzcollab-approaches}

The right level of infrastructure is itself a judgment. Excessive
infrastructure on a small project is busywork; insufficient
infrastructure on a large one is technical debt. A compendium is
overkill for interactive exploration, for a one-off script, for a
teaching example whose point is the code, and for a quick
reproduction of someone else's analysis, whose structure should
control. It is the right weight for a collaborative analysis
passed between team members, for one that must survive months or
years after its lead analyst has moved on, and for any analysis
subject to the federal requirements of @sec-federal. A tool that
makes the heavy path cheap moves the right answer toward more
infrastructure on the margin, but never removes the need to
decide.

Whichever path you take, the group's conventions (a preferred
database client, a set of in-house packages, a journal's Quarto
template) are best written down once, in a template project or a
shared lockfile, so that every new project inherits them rather
than re-enumerating them.

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'}
**Question.** A colleague argues that adopting a framework makes
the pillar audit unnecessary, since the framework writes every
file. What is wrong with the argument?

**Answer.** A framework writes the pillars once, at scaffolding
time; the audit checks them now. Lockfiles drift as packages are
installed, a Dockerfile's base tag falls behind a lockfile
snapshotted under a newer R, and data change after the manifest is
written. Each failure in @tbl-five-pillars can occur in a
scaffolded project as easily as in a hand-built one.
:::

### Exercises

3. For each project below, choose an approach from
   @tbl-zzcollab-approaches and name the pillar you would check
   most often: (a) a one-off descriptive table for a clinician's
   abstract; (b) a two-year trial analysis passed between three
   analysts; (c) a methods paper with a simulation study.

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'}
(a) A script, with no compendium; if the abstract becomes a paper,
promote it then. (b) A framework that makes every project in the
group look alike, `zzcollab` or a group template, with the data
pillar checked most often, because extracts arrive throughout the
trial. (c) `rrtools` or a hand-built compendium; the pillar to
watch is the environment (Dockerfile and lockfile together),
because simulation results depend on the random-number generator
and numerical libraries. Other defensible answers exist; the
reasoning should tie the approach to the project's lifetime and
number of hands.
:::

## Optional: automating the assembly with zzcollab {#sec-zzcollab-optional}

This section is optional. `zzcollab` is the author's in-house
framework (@sec-lab-software), one way to automate the assembly
beside `rrtools` and `workflowr`; nothing else in the book
depends on it. It packages the ideas of `rrtools`, `renv`, and
Docker into one command-line workflow, trading control over the
layout for speed of setup and uniformity across a group's
projects. It does not call `rrtools`; it writes its own layout,
modeled on the same compendium.[^zzcollab-version]

[^zzcollab-version]: Described as of the repository at
    `github.com/rgt47/zzcollab` in October 2026. Profiles, `make`
    targets, and the bundle schema have changed between versions;
    check the repository's `CHANGELOG.md` and `make help` before
    relying on the details below.

### The first-project walkthrough

The minimum `zzcollab` session (display-only):

```bash
mkdir hfhome-analysis
cd hfhome-analysis
zzc tidyverse             # scaffold (Five Pillars appear)
make r                    # enter R session inside Docker
                          # ... do analysis ...
make check-renv           # validate dependencies
make docker-render-qmd    # render the Quarto report
```

**`zzc tidyverse`** runs the framework's
scaffolding. After it completes, the directory
contains a `DESCRIPTION`, `R/`, `analysis/`, and
`tests/` directories, a Quarto report at
`analysis/report/index.qmd`, a minimal `renv.lock`, a
`Dockerfile` on the `rocker/tidyverse` base, and a
`Makefile`. It then offers to build the image. Git is
a separate step (`zzc git`, or `git init` yourself).
The generated Dockerfile pins the rocker base image by tag and,
when Docker can resolve it, by digest (for example
`rocker/r-ver:4.6.0@sha256:...`).

**`make r`** drops you into an interactive R session
inside the container, with the project directory
mounted, so files edited inside the container persist
on the host. It does not build the image; if no image
exists it says so and falls back to R on the host.
Build first with `make docker-build` if you declined at
scaffolding time.

**`make check-renv`** runs
`zzrenvcheck::check_packages(auto_fix = TRUE,
strict = TRUE)` on the host. It checks that the
packages your code uses, the packages `DESCRIPTION`
declares, and the packages `renv.lock` records all
agree, and with `auto_fix` it *edits* `DESCRIPTION` and
`renv.lock` to add what is missing. It is not a
read-only audit; use `make check-renv-no-fix` for a
report that changes nothing. It does not build the
Dockerfile or inspect `.Rprofile` or the data.

**`make docker-render-qmd`** runs
`quarto render analysis/report/index.qmd` inside the
container. (`make docker-render` renders an R Markdown
report instead, `analysis/report/report.Rmd` by
default.)

### The project `Makefile`

Every `zzcollab` project gets a `Makefile` with many targets;
`make help` lists them. The ones used most:

| Target | Action |
|---|---|
| `make help` | List all targets |
| `make r` | Drop into R inside the project's container |
| `make rstudio` | Launch RStudio Server (port 8787) |
| `make docker-render-qmd` | Render `analysis/report/index.qmd` in the container |
| `make check-renv` | Validate dependencies and add missing ones |
| `make check-renv-no-fix` | Validate dependencies without modifying files |
| `make snapshot` | Snapshot `renv.lock` in the container, then validate |
| `make docker-build` | Rebuild the image (use after adding packages) |
| `make hash-data` | Write a SHA-256 manifest of the raw-data directory |
| `make verify-data` | Check the raw data against that manifest |
| `make clean` | Remove package build artifacts |

: Common `zzcollab` `make` targets. {#tbl-zzcollab-make}

`make hash-data` writes `data-manifest.sha256` in the same
`shasum` format as the manifest in @sec-zzcollab-audit, so
`audit_pillars()` reads either. `make docker-build` rebuilds the
image after you add packages or system dependencies; `make r`
silently uses the old image until you do. `make clean` removes
package build artifacts (`*.tar.gz` and `*.Rcheck`); it does not
touch rendered reports or Quarto's `_freeze/` directory.

`make rstudio` is for browser-based work. Open
`http://localhost:8787` and log in as `rstudio` with the password
`rstudio`, which the target prints. The target publishes port
8787 on all of your machine's network interfaces, so with that
fixed password, use it only on a trusted network (see
@sec-docker for binding to `127.0.0.1` instead).

### Choosing a profile

The command `zzc <profile>`, run inside an empty project
directory, scaffolds a project using one of four profiles, and a
profile's main job is to choose the rocker base image:

| Profile | Base image | Approximate size | Use |
|---|---|---|---|
| `minimal` | `rocker/r-ver` | 650 MB | Command-line work, continuous integration |
| `tidyverse` | `rocker/tidyverse` | 1.2 GB | Tidyverse data analysis |
| `rstudio` | `rocker/rstudio` | 980 MB | RStudio Server development |
| `publishing` | `rocker/verse` | 4.2 GB | Manuscripts that need LaTeX |

: `zzcollab` profiles. {#tbl-zzcollab-profiles}

The `tidyverse` profile was formerly called `analysis`, and
`zzc analysis` still works as a deprecated alias. There are no
modeling or Shiny profiles; for those needs the framework's own
advice is to start from one of the four and add packages inside
the container. The profile is a substantive choice: a manuscript
that must render to PDF needs LaTeX, which only the `publishing`
profile's base image has, while a simple descriptive analysis in
the `publishing` profile waits for a 4 GB image it does not need.

Modeling packages need no special profile. Install
`lme4` or `survival` inside the container, record them
with `make snapshot`, and rebuild with
`make docker-build`. When zzcollab generates the
Dockerfile it reads the packages your code, `DESCRIPTION`,
and `renv.lock` mention and adds the system libraries
they need, so a profile mismatch costs a rebuild rather
than a hand-edited `apt-get` line.

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'}
**Question.** You are scaffolding a project that will fit a Cox
proportional hazards model with `survival::coxph()` and a
mixed-effects model with `lme4::glmer()`, then render the result
as a PDF manuscript. Which profile?

**Answer.** `publishing`, because the PDF manuscript is the one
requirement a profile actually supplies: it is the only profile
whose base image includes LaTeX. The modeling packages are not a
profile question at all. Install `lme4` and `survival` inside the
container, run `make snapshot` so that `renv.lock` and
`DESCRIPTION` record them, and rebuild. Neither package needs an
extra system library; `survival` is a recommended package that
ships with R.
:::

### Bundles and extension

Profiles are defined in the repository's
`templates/bundles.yaml`, which has three sections:
`library_bundles` name sets of system packages, `package_bundles`
name sets of R packages, and `profiles` combine a base image with
one bundle of each. There is no `inherits` key, and the quickstart
command accepts only the four built-in profile names. A group that
wants different defaults can add a profile entry in a fork and
select it with `zzc docker --profile <name>`, but the Dockerfile
generator reads only the entry's `base_image`; system libraries
come from the packages the project uses, and R packages are added
inside the container and recorded with `make snapshot`. Group
conventions therefore belong in a template project or a shared
`renv.lock`, as for any other approach, not in a new profile.

### Exercises

4. Scaffold a `zzcollab` project in a scratch directory, copy the
   two HF-HOME files into `analysis/data/raw_data/`, run
   `make hash-data`, and audit the result with `audit_pillars()`.
   (This needs Docker and the `zzc` command, and creates a project
   on your machine.)

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'}
A complete scaffold passes every row except, until you commit, the
source-code row's Git check (`zzc git` or `git init`). If the
Dockerfile row fails, compare its `FROM` line with the lockfile's
`R$Version`: the two were written at different times, and the fix
is to rebuild with `make docker-build` after a snapshot, not to
edit the tag by hand. Run `make check-renv-no-fix` as well; unlike
`make check-renv`, it changes nothing.
:::

## Rules of thumb

1. **Habit 1: the compendium is the unit.** Code, data,
   environment, and document travel together; audit all five
   pillars, not the ones a tool happens to write.
2. **Habit 4: pin the environment.** The lockfile and the
   Dockerfile pin different layers, and they must agree on the
   R version.
3. **Habit 2: raw data are evidence.** Commit a checksum manifest,
   and change it only when new data arrive deliberately.

## Cumulative practice

5. *Cumulative (uses @sec-renv and @sec-docker).* Assemble a
   compendium by hand for an analysis of the two HF-HOME files:
   the `rrtools` layout, `renv` with a snapshot, the canonical
   Dockerfile with its tag set from the lockfile, and a data
   manifest. Run `audit_pillars()` until every row passes, then
   build the image and render the report inside it from a fresh
   clone.
6. *On your own work (no key).* Audit a project of yours with
   `audit_pillars()`, and record for each failing pillar what it
   would take to close it and whether you think it is worth it.

## Cheat sheet

| Pillar | File | Create with | Check with |
|---|---|---|---|
| Dockerfile | `Dockerfile`, `.dockerignore` | Copy from @sec-docker-canonical | Base tag equals `renv::lockfile_read("renv.lock")$R$Version` |
| `renv.lock` | `renv.lock` | `renv::init()`, `renv::snapshot()` | `renv::status()` |
| `.Rprofile` | `.Rprofile` | `renv::init()` | `.libPaths()[1]` from the render directory |
| Source code | `R/`, `analysis/` | `rrtools::use_compendium()`, `git init` | `git status`; `git tag` |
| Data | `analysis/data/raw_data/`, `data-manifest.sha256` | `cli::hash_file_sha256()`, or `make hash-data` | `shasum -a 256 --check data-manifest.sha256` |
| All five | | | `audit_pillars(".")` |

: The Five Pillars at a glance. {#tbl-zzcollab-cheat-sheet}

- [@marwick2018packaging], the conceptual framing of the research
  compendium that every approach in this chapter inherits.
- [@boettiger2017rocker], the `rocker` images on which the

## Prerequisites answers {#sec-quiz-answers-10}

1. The Five Pillars are: (1) a **Dockerfile** (captures the
   operating system and system libraries), (2) an **renv.lock**
   (captures R package versions), (3) an **.Rprofile** (activates
   renv and sets project-local R options), (4) **source code** (the
   actual analysis), and (5) **data** (raw and processed, or a
   documented access path when data cannot be shared). Each pillar
   captures a layer that the others do not: Docker covers the
   operating system below R, `renv` covers the R packages,
   `.Rprofile` covers R's runtime configuration, source code is the
   work product, and data is the input. Remove any one and the
   analysis cannot be reproduced.
2. It still has to pin the source code and the data. The code is
   pinned when it is committed and the reported version tagged;
   the data, when the files are in the repository or a committed
   checksum manifest records them. Nobody notices their absence
   until a rerun gives a different answer, which is why the audit
   in @sec-zzcollab-audit checks for them explicitly.
3. A framework is worth adopting when many projects should look
   alike or the setup will be repeated often; for a single paper,
   assembling by hand or with `rrtools` is enough. Every framework
   writes the pillars once. Keeping them consistent afterwards
   (lockfile, Dockerfile tag, data manifest) is still yours, and
   the audit is how you check it. `zzcollab` *wraps* `renv` and
   Docker and *follows* `rrtools`'s layout without calling it.
